The best GTA 6 Easter eggs, from Mario hats to a time travel portal to Vice City

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In our interviews with Rockstar Games' art team, we've explored GTA VI's environmental storytelling and the building design in GTA VI.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In our interviews with Rockstar Games' art team, we've explored GTA VI's environmental storytelling and the building design in GTA VI. Now that players are in the game and exploring the huge world that is Leonida, it's apparent that the attention to detail also extends to some wonderful hidden references.

Recent findings suggest that from past game callbacks to supernatural encounters, pop culture references and elaborate optional missions, the GTA VI Easter eggs are another example of how the game rewards deep exploration (also see our GTA 6 review). Here are a few of the best we've seen so far. Let me know your favourite.

Spoiler warning! If you want to discover GTA VI Easter eggs in your own time, stop reading and go back to the game.

I discovered this GTA 6 easter egg about 3 days ago, here it is in video form, I think I'm the first person to ever crack this code in the world so enjoy! #GTA6 https://t.co/vTORjUlYNiNovember 23, 2026.

We've put on a spoiler warning above, but I think most people would need to be putting in some serious hours of play to ever come across this one, which has to be the most elaborate GTA VI Easter egg that's been found so far.

As revealed by Memeio above, the Vice City portal Easter egg is a wildly complex multi-step time-travel secret with some very subtle clues, including "a sound effect from Vice City" when you power up the radio tower in Key Lento and individual letters that spell out a Vice City cheat code. The portal takes Jason back to a PS2-era version of the Malibu Club from the 2002 Grand Theft Auto: Vice City. Completing it unlocks Tommy Vercetti's Hawaiian shirt and motorcycle.

Industry observers note that GTA 6 might not be coming to the Switch, but Rockstar at least indicates some love for Nintendo with its Mario Easter egg. Head north and seek out the ruined brick and stone building in the woods of southwest Moreau, Lummox County.

Using the bong on the blue-tarp crate in the middle of the ruins triggers a trip and spawns a translucent floating block that you can jump on or shoot to break, mimicking Mario breaking a Question Mark Block. The prize is a pair of Mario and Luigi-style hats marked "J" for Jason and "L" for Lucia.

Don't forget to check out the best Nintendo Switch Black Friday deals.

Heard what I thought was a tiger or lion on the way to the Grassrivers, found the Skunk Ape instead... #GTAVI #GTA6 https://t.co/dMDfCXHxLZNovember 20, 2026.

Sources indicate that in the Gullet Marsh, Grassrivers and around Cottonmouth Lake, players have come across a piece of Florida folklore: Skunk Ape, the state's version of Bigfoot. A Weazel News report about sightings plays on the TV in Jason's house, and cryptid hunter Kirk offers a 'Search for the Skunk Ape' side mission available at night. I won't say what happens if you kill it, but things get weird.

Continuing a gag from Vice City, Rockstar has again included an actual Easter egg, but finding it isn't easy: you have to spend seven minutes just climbing the tallest radio tower in Vice-Dale Country for no other reason than to reach a bird's nest laden with eggs (and to enjoy a short cut scene).

According to recent reports, vice City is based on Miami, home to TV's favourite vigilante serial killer Dexter Morgan, and GTA 6 has several references to the show. You can find a dupe of his apartment in Trinity Apartments, Washington Island, near the Top Fun Drones shop at Vice Beach. Up on the roof, there's a toolbox, with a syringe, a knife, duct tape and rope.

In a recent development, GTA 6’s jet-skiing dog Easter egg is a reference to Loosy, a real-life dog from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, who regularly rides jet skis Around her local area! 🐕🌴 @thrill_com https://t.co/7489XDBHYYNovember 19, 2026.

Early in the game, Jason can go swimming near his house and if you go far enough, you'll encounter the surprising sight of a German shepherd riding a jet ski. It's been suggested that this is a nod to a real dog in Fort Lauderdale, a golden retriever known for his fondness for riding waves.

A post shared by Kyle Soto Underwater Photography (@kylesoto).

Recent findings suggest that GTA VI also appears to feature a real dive spot under a lighthouse off the Florida keys, and yes, someone's been out there to make a video comparing the in-game location with the real thing (see above). The conclusion is that the real thing is cooler, but it's still an impressively realistic detail.

That remarked, a marine biologist has noted that Rockstar's attention to authentic detail slips a little bit in GTA VI's underwater scenes (see the post below).

A post shared by Underwater Filmmaker & Host (@dr.shireenrahimi).

Ok GTA 6 is nuts. I went exploring and swimming in the north of the island and I got taken hostage by a Saw-like character who released me into a Hunger Games-esque arena to be hunted down by people with night-vision goggles and dogs in tactical vests. https://t.co/58l74dr6QNNovember 19, 2026.

Sources indicate that while the Easter egg above has been likened to Saw and Hunger Games, some will recognise it as a reference to Rockstar's 2003 stealth game Manhunt. You'll need to swim around Hyde Island to get kidnapped, knocked out and imprisoned with a detonation device on your neck. After the countdown, prepare to gather ammunition as you get hunted in the dark.

According to recent reports, given all the things that people have found in less than a week since the game's release, it make me wonder what other, potentially even more complicated GTA VI Easter Eggs are hiding waiting to be discovered. Let me know below if you've found any.

Museums finding upcoming ways to measure wellness initiatives’ value

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Museum programming in the US has been branching out recently, much of it in the direction of connecting art to health and wellbeing.
  • Recent findings suggest that the qualitative data from a caregiver's perspective does not necessarily include the point-of-view of the person struggling with cognitive decline.
  • It has been revealed that the Frye is at the forefront of art and health initiatives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Museum programming in the US has been branching out recently, much of it in the direction of connecting art to health and wellbeing. As part of this trend, institutions have been creating programmes for people living with memory loss. But these present unique challenges, particularly when it comes to evaluating their success.

Recent findings suggest that the qualitative data from a caregiver's perspective does not necessarily include the point-of-view of the person struggling with cognitive decline. This is why institutions like Seattle’s Frye Art Museum try to do a lot of in-the-moment observations and feedback rather than relying exclusively on formal surveys.

It has been revealed that the Frye is at the forefront of art and health initiatives. Each quarter, the museum offers a special programme for medical residents, students and teaching professionals from nearby hospitals, designed to develop perspective-taking and empathy. Meanwhile the museum recently expanded its Creative Aging initiative, gallery-based experiences and hands-on artmaking in partnership with the University of Washington's Memory and Brain Wellness Center.

Industry observers note that located in Seattle’s First Hill neighbourhood and surrounded by medical centres and senior living facilities, the Frye has served older adults experiencing memory loss for 17 years. Its Creative Aging programme began with a former employee’s experience caring for her mother with dementia, and has since expanded to reach broader communities of older adults.

The Frye's experience in the field highlights a broader challenge facing museums as arts-and-health programming expands. The Lancet medical journal recently published a call for translating growing evidence of the arts’ health benefits into more equitable access, stronger healthcare partnerships and research into how programmes work in practice. For museums, a big question is how to evaluate these initiatives while responding to community needs.

Participants at one of the Frye’s Creative Aging programmes Photo: Runyon Colie, courtesy the Frye Art Museum, Seattle.

Susan Magsamen, the founder and executive director of the International Arts + Mind Lab at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, sees this kind of programming as an opportunity for museums to expand their public roles. She describes art as “a superpower that we have forgotten” and museums as institutions that contribute to “human thriving and flourishing”.

Magsamen compares the growing integration of health and wellbeing into museum missions with the emergence of education as a core museum function in previous decades. “Beyond things like attendance, revenue and membership, we need to think about a scorecard,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “What is the institutional performance and public benefits?”.

The Frye has been using the Art Bridges Foundation’s Art + Wellness Toolkit, which includes validated measures across four areas of wellbeing: social, emotional, cognitive and physical. The museum is right now evaluating four programmes, incorporating the toolkit's terminology into its materials and developing surveys using its standardised measures.

“This common language has been valuable as we grow programmes under art and wellbeing," claims Lea Lovelace, the Frye’s associate director of creative aging programmes.

In a recent development, jill Sonke, a co-author of the Lancet study, underscores the importance of measuring behavior and patterns of engagement, so that the most vulnerable can access the arts and their underlying health benefits. “Institutions need to also measure who’s not coming,” she claims, “why they don’t see themselves in the programming.”.

According to recent reports, in the swiftly developing field, Sonke cautions museum staff to move ahead carefully. Enthusiasm for evidence can create its own problems. If institutions set out primarily to prove that their programmes work, evaluation instruments can inadvertently be designed to confirm the outcome they hope to find. “We need to make sure that we’re designing objective, open measures that will allow us to really understand the experiences of the people we’re seeking to serve,” she states.

One of the Frye’s Creative Aging programmes Photo: Runyon Colie, courtesy the Frye Art Museum, Seattle.

Sonke also questions whether additional assessment is always warranted: “If the evidence exists already, if it’s not really necessary, then it’s not ethical to put people through the burden of assessment.".

The Frye has experienced these tensions firsthand. "It's a balancing act," claims Tamar Benzikry, the museum’s director of learning and engagement. "We are careful about 'survey fatigue', because we realise you might not get the information requested because our audience is burnt out from surveys.".

Sonke, despite her caution, underscores the importance of “making relationships and normalising the idea that museums should be talking to public health folks, and public health folks should absolutely be talking to museums”.

In a recent development, the Frye is always working with community leaders to identify barriers to participation and create programmes that strengthen connections between the museum, public health and healthcare. The team intends to share experiences at a convening of museum professionals next May, while incorporating arts and health more deeply into its 2027 exhibition programme.

Activities will include gallery-based creative movement inspired by works of art and led by a physician who is also a trained dancer. There are also aims for folklore-inspired slow-looking and storytelling sessions led by a professional storyteller with training in gerontology.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mucho's Biotic brand identity grows from a single dot into a living system, turning one synthetic cell into many through reaction-diffusion.
  • Biotic is a nonprofit stewarding SpudCell, a synthetic cell built from scratch rather than modified from an existing one.
  • The wordmark pairs the dot with lowercase biotic in Roobert Medium, the primary typeface, with Medium as the default weight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mucho's Biotic brand identity grows from a single dot into a living system, turning one synthetic cell into many through reaction-diffusion.

Biotic is a nonprofit stewarding SpudCell, a synthetic cell built from scratch rather than modified from an existing one. Mucho answers that science with a mark as plain as the idea behind it: one black dot, the simplest shape a single cell can take. From that dot the identity grows. Reaction-diffusion software built by Karl Sims lets the pattern branch, split and multiply across every surface, so the same dot that opens the website also fills a stage screen, a tote bag and a stack of business cards. Black and white carry the whole system, with a lime accent kept for small moments like the arrow buttons on the site.

The wordmark pairs the dot with lowercase biotic in Roobert Medium, the primary typeface, with Medium as the default weight. Headlines run large and plain, often as a single statement across a page: Out of one, many. on a phone screen, Building the Operating System for Accessible Biology on the community page. Dotted rules divide sections instead of solid lines, a quiet nod to cells lining up in a row. The grid stays open and calm, with wide black fields and white panels trading places down the page.

The system proves itself on paper and cloth. Business cards stack in a grid, each one carrying a different reaction-diffusion circle and the line Out of one, many. Three black booklets carry white circles and three short lines: Propagating possibility. Building biology. Honoring Humanity. A white tote prints one large circle under the small dot wordmark. The guidelines show the next phase too, with the same circles in blue, green and purple, color held back until the science is ready for it. On the website, a live clock counts down to 2050, the year Biotic calls Bloomsday, when the world may no longer produce enough resources for its growing population.

This optical illusion has stumped scientists for decades, and things just got weirder

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (587 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, we love a good optical illusion, and we've seen plenty of mind-benders over the years, but there's one really famous one that continues to intrigue scientists.
  • A lot of people see it that way, but some people don't.
  • This optical illusion was named after Franz Carl Müller-Lyer, its creator.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we love a good optical illusion, and we've seen plenty of mind-benders over the years, but there's one really famous one that continues to intrigue scientists. The Müller-Lyer illusion looks so simple: two lines, one with arrows pointing inwards from the ends and one with arrows pointing out. One looks longer than the other, right?

A lot of people see it that way, but some people don't. Some people can immediately tell that the two horizontal lines are actually the same length (see below if you don't believe me). But the reason for this difference in perfection continues to be a topic of massive debate.

This optical illusion was named after Franz Carl Müller-Lyer, its creator. Many people initially assume that the line with the arrows pointing inwards is longer than the other. But then research published in the 1960s claimed that people in African and Southeast Asian countries weren't so often fooled by the illusion. It seemed that WEIRD people were mode susceptible – that is, people whose backgrounds were Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich and from a Democracy.

That led to a theory that the apparent difference might have something to do with people in industrialised societies being more exposed to sharp angles and straight lines when growing up, and that this somehow moulds their perception.

The problem is that the suggested difference in perception has now been called into question. As reported by Sciencing, Dorsa Amir and Chaz Firestone, anthropologists at Duke and John Hopkins, have gathered evidence opposing the theory developed in the 1960s and published their findings in the Psychological Review.

They note that many variation of the Müller-Lyer illusion have been developed, including ones that work in a similar way despite using curved lines instead of straight ones. Other similar illusions abound, including the Ebbinghaus illusion, in which two identical dots are perceived to be different sizes depending on whether they're surrounded by six large dots or eight small dots. In that case, there are no lines or angles at all.

Amir and Firestone also turned up flaws in the case studies from the 1960s, and found that later reports had misconstrued the original findings. The evidence that Africans and Asians aren't fooled by the Müller-Lyer illusion appeared to be very scant.

In a recent development, but one discovery would seem to be even more conclusive in disproving the old WEIRD theory. The optical illusion has been tested on people who were born blind and later had lens replacement surgery, and it appears to trick people immediately after they gain sight despite them not having grown up seeing lines and angles around them.

With the WEIRD theory ruled out, it seems then that this old optical illusion has become weirder, becoming a mystery again.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kaleidoscopic patterns adorn the exterior of this pavilion in Doha, Qatar, designed by artist Gerhard Richter with US studio Selldorf Architects as an art gallery.
  • Simply called Doha Pavilion, the psychedelic structure was conceived a work of both art and architecture for MIA Park – a public space outside the Museum of Islamic Art by IM Pei.
  • It serves as a permanent pavilion for the site and as a gallery for Richter’s own work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Iwan Baan.

Kaleidoscopic patterns adorn the exterior of this pavilion in Doha, Qatar, designed by artist Gerhard Richter with US studio Selldorf Architects as an art gallery.

Simply called Doha Pavilion, the psychedelic structure was conceived a work of both art and architecture for MIA Park – a public space outside the Museum of Islamic Art by IM Pei.

It serves as a permanent pavilion for the site and as a gallery for Richter’s own work.

Richter designed the Doha Pavilion with Selldorf Architects as a reference to his Strip paintings – a series that involved digitally dividing his Abstract Painting artwork into vertical stripes, building on his earlier explorations of colour, pattern and repetition.

“My trip to Doha in 2013 came two years into developing my Strip paintings, and the city’s architecture and history sparked an idea for a pavilion that could unite the thematic threads of that body of work,” said Richter.

“The pavilion’s exterior features decorative tiles based on the patterns that first led me to the Strips,” he continued. “Doha is the right place and the only place for my pavilion.”.

Doha Pavilion has a six-sided form, wrapped in psychedelic tiles displaying repeating, kaleidoscopic patterns that recall geometries seen in Islamic art, nodding to the project’s context.

Selldorf Architects founder Annabelle Selldorf said the design reflects a “profound culmination of many years of [Richter’s] research into abstraction”.

“I am grateful for the welcome that Gerhard Richter extended to me, and for the wonderful dialogue that ensued, as my studio made manifest the work that had existed in his mind,” she mentioned.

“This pavilion is the profound culmination of many years of his research into abstraction, with intensely physical patterns that invite you to immerse yourself in their endlessness,” she continued.

“The more I look at them, the more fascinating they become to me as an architectural space to experience.”.

Recent findings suggest that inside, Richter’s paintings and sculptures are displayed throughout the hexagonal gallery space. This includes both archival and new works made especially for the pavilion.

Among the fresh works is the Strip Tower – a freestanding tripartite sculpture.

The opening of Doha Pavilion coincides with the inaugural edition of Rubaiya Qatar 2026, which is an international visual arts quadrennial.

It has been revealed that elsewhere, Selldorf Architects recently completed the controversial remodel of the National Gallery’s Sainsbury Wing. In an interview with Dezeen after the opening, founder Selldorf said that “what matters is I know why we did things”.

Photography by Iwan Baan.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A collection of showcases, old and newly introduced, took place in New York this November, effectively adding a second design week to a city already loaded with events. Dezeen’s US editor Ben Dreith explores the offerings.

The as-yet-unofficial design week in the first weeks of November came into focus earlier this year, when trade fair ICFF, anchor fair of NYCxDesign, announced that in 2027 it will take place simultaneously with sister fair BDNY, which has been held in November for years.

The move has prompted questions in the city about the future of the NYCxDesign festival in May and what a November design week would look like.

While BDNY and high-end showcase Salon Art + Design have always been held in November, other design fairs have sprouted to take advantage of the opportunity to show during this busy period.

The week is positioning itself, without any explicit organisation, as a massive event in the New York design calendar.

Even NYCxDesign, still scheduled for May as usual in 2027, held a November event bringing in designers Ross Lovegrove, Karim Rashid and Rem D Koolhaas for a talk moderated by Newly introduced York-based design writer Camille Okhio.

It has been revealed that the panellists spoke about the potential for AI and derided the inclusion of craft in conversations about design. However, as writer Debika Ray noted in an opinion piece for Dezeen, crafted, one-off pieces have lately come to dominate design shows.

NYCxDesign staking out a talk with well-known industrial designers suggests that its May event could be devoted to industrial design, while November complements it with a focus on collectible furniture.

This was definitely true this year, when collectible designs dominated the November showcases.

In a recent development, among these was the Brussels-founded design fair Collectible. For its third Latest York iteration, it moved from office tower-turned creative hub WSA to a former movie theatre on the Upper East Side that is being developed by entities related to WSA.

While the space fit the experimental nature of the work, the execution was, by some accounts, somewhat chaotic, with one exhibitor staff member being sent to the hospital after an unstable light fell onto her head as the exhibitors were installing it in their booth.

Collectible called it an “isolated occurrence involving an exhibitor’s equipment”.

“The safety of our exhibitors, staff and visitors is a priority, and we take any reported incident seriously,” a representative for Collectible told Dezeen.

“Collectible maintains safety procedures for the fair and expects all exhibitors to ensure that their own equipment is installed and secured appropriately.”.

However, the fair also had some strong showings. Philadelphia-based Dudd Haus highlighted a pared-down booth with its usual mix of conceptual one-offs. Particularly of note was a milled-aluminium floor lamp by Jordan Maurice and a paravent made with telephone cords by Overt Cove.

Also eye-catching was a booth of droopy glass lamps and shades with erotic overtones by Upstate New York gallery Freaks, and another sensual booth with drapes and lacquered furniture by Iitem studio.

The fair’s scenography carried the sleek, modern, USM-laden feel from the prior additions. Curators Alex Tieghi-Walker and Lynette Nylander designed special sections.

Bas-reliefs were popular on otherwise modern furniture, including a battened screen by Polish studio Wiktoria & Filip Bielicki for Objekt Gallery and a coffee table with raised ceramic on its base by Small Things Studio for Salon 21.

At Collectible, Montreal design collective Ensemble showcased its members’ work on nooks in a wall made with USM panels.

This was just a taste of what Ensemble had in store for the week. The collective brought their signature experimentation to Yabu Pushelberg’s Tribeca studio, creating a plywood room-within-a-room to showcase work, including newly introduced lamps by Zebulon Perron, sculptural glass lamps by Alex Joncas, metal works by Jérémy Paguet, leather lamps by Jeta Studio and brass-lined mirrors by Jeremy Le Chatelier.

It was an extremely focused showing that proved sometimes you can do more with less.

At Salon Art + Design, a few younger galleries stuck out from the historical work and ultra-high-end designs that usually characterise the fair.

Brooklyn-based Zarolat’s showing included ash-wood lamps with cellulose shades by Natural Urbano and Polybion, while Latest York-based hub for Brazilian furniture, Bossa Furniture, showcased a greatest hits of mid-century São Paulo makers, including Joaquim Tenreiro.

It has been revealed that BDNY was, as usual, where most of the actual commerce took place during the week. While the interior designers and architects descended on the sample-forward showing, a few brands indicated stand-out collections, including Sancal’s showing of Júlia Esqué’s playfully fringed armchairs and Santa & Cole’s modern, fun lighting.

Later in the week, LA-based Basic Space, run by the organisers behind Design Miami, returned to SoHo. With artistic direction by Alexander May, the stark, white-cube approach differed from the in-situ, multi-room afair that characterised the first Newly introduced York Basic Space in 2025.

The fair featured a focus on big names and multiple co-curators competing for attention on the promotional materials and in the execution.

Standout pieces included the live-edge wood furniture with small metal connective elements by Brooklyn-based designer Gregory Beson, as well as Daniel Swarilov’s metal credenzas, in a section curated by Marquel Williams.

Sources indicate that paris-based Harry Nuriev created a metallic take on first-class airline seats as a standalone installation. Another booth featured an oversized sofa by NFL player Stefon Diggs’ luxury furniture brand Si Vis Pacem, illustrating the fair’s mix of design with celebrity culture.

Finally, Mexico City-based creative studio Fábrica, run by artist Darryl Richardson and partner Maryah Ananda, held its La Sala showcase in a loft near Penn Station.

With a focus on international Black designers, the showcase featured art and design, with the space shaped like a living room by interior designer Johnathan Bailey.

Furniture pieces of note included a slim metal chair by Kai Avent-deLeo and an armchair by Mark Grattan.

The social focus of the event gave it an aesthetic heft, and a few of its stated goals, “community over curation” and “warmth over spectacle”, made it stand out from many of the other offerings from the week.

Judging by the willingness of the different fall fairs to join in, it seems likely that the November design week will fully take off.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that two men accused of the murder of the South African mixed-media artist and curator Tamlin Blake appeared in the Riebeek West magistrate’s court on Wednesday (25 November). Blake was found killed on Sunday at her home in Riebeek-West, a small town 80km northwest of Cape Town. The 51-year-old artist was a well-loved member of the town’s prominent community of artists, among whom she lived for the past 20 years.

The two suspects, Pedro Fraser and Ronnie Von Wielligh, both aged 32, have been charged with murder and possession of stolen goods and will appear in court again on 1 December where they are expected to respond to the charges.

Angry protestors gathered outside the court, demanding justice with some chanting “no bail!”, reported the South African digital news platform, News24.

A representative for the state told the court that the murder was a Schedule 6 offence, which is one of the most serious categories of crime, according to News24. Prosecutors reportedly stated she was attacked with a sharp object. Fraser and Von Wielligh will remain in prison until their appearance next Tuesday.

The police tracked down the suspects after tracing Blake’s cellphone, which was allegedly stolen during the attack, a source told another news platform, IOL Media.

Industry observers note that “One suspect was arrested in possession of the cellphone. During police questioning, he admitted that he did not commit the offence alone. He then took police to his co-accused,” IOL Media’s source remarked.

The residents of Riebeek West and neighbouring Riebeek Kasteel are “completely shell shocked” by the news of Blake’s death, a fellow local artist and close friend of Blake’s, Kevan Moses, tells The Art Newspaper. He describes the area as home to many artists, “international, established as well as upcoming” and that it is a “very nurturing creative environment”.

Blake, who was born in Johannesburg, obtained a master’s in fine arts at the University of Stellenbosch in 2001. She has exhibited extensively at home and abroad and is represented by Everard Read Gallery, which has locations in South Africa and London.

Blake was, according to her website, instrumental in developing beading techniques which are now used by various South African artists. Her recent works include tapestries woven from recycled hand-spun newspaper. She was also the chief curator for the Spier Arts Trust, a Cape Town-based organisation dedicated to building sustainable careers for professional artists. There Blake oversaw the acquisition of works of art for diverse collections and lead initiatives that supported artists at pivotal stages of their careers.

Recent findings suggest that “Tamlin was a remarkable artist whose work reflected a deep sensitivity to the natural world and an unwavering commitment to her creative practice,” Everard Read Gallery said in a statement. “Through her distinctive voice and vision, she built a respected career and touched the lives of collectors, colleagues, and fellow artists in South Africa and abroad.

“We are grateful to have worked with Tamlin over many years, and to have shared her work with our audiences. Her contribution to contemporary South African art will be remembered with admiration, gratitude and affection.”.

Spier Arts Trust described Blake in a statement as a “visionary artist” who “possessed the rarest gift: a boundless, ego-free generosity that put other people’s growth and dignity at the centre of her life’s work”.

“Those of us fortunate enough to have worked alongside her will forever remember her sharp eye, her quiet grace, her advocacy for authentic, exceptional expression, and the warmth she brought into every studio conversation,” the trust mentioned.

Her friend Moses mentioned: “Tamlin was a great artist, the gentlest person and a quiet thought leader. She was a mentor for many artists. She will be truly missed.”.

Blake leaves behind her husband and two daughters, aged 18 and 20.

Alien Breed 35th Anniversary Collection review: A brilliant slice of gaming history

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alien Breed 35th Anniversary Collection is a fascinating archive of Team17's early years, filled with art and developer insights, even if not all the games deserve a return visit.
  • Virtual Museum is packed with art, interviews and unreleased projects.
  • According to recent reports, why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alien Breed 35th Anniversary Collection is a fascinating archive of Team17's early years, filled with art and developer insights, even if not all the games deserve a return visit.

Six Amiga-era Alien Breed games in one package.

Virtual Museum is packed with art, interviews and unreleased projects.

Twin-stick controls, CRT filters and save states.

Local co-op, online Rush Mode and solo Horde Mode.

The 3D games feel like historical curiosities.

Early top-down games can be punishingly difficult.

According to recent reports, why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Publisher: Commodore International.

Release date: 24 September 2026.

Format: PS5 (reviewed), Xbox Series X/S, PC.

How to buy: Digitally on the PS Store, Xbox Store, Steam.

It has been revealed that some games you remember as brilliant, and others you remember as brilliant because you were 12, sitting in front of an Amiga with a joystick in one hand and a pile of floppy disks beside you. Alien Breed is probably a bit of both.

According to recent reports, team17's sci-fi shooter celebrates its 35th anniversary with this newly introduced collection, bringing together six games from the series' original Amiga era (read my Apidya review for more Amiga gaming). That's quite a lot of history in one package, taking in the original top-down shooters and the later, more ambitious attempts to bring the series into the 3D era.

And there's a lot to like about the way this collection has been assembled. Alongside the games is an interactive archive filled with original artwork, developer interviews, soundtracks, design documents and even material from Alien Breed projects that never made it to release. It's a proper look back at a British studio finding its feet during one of gaming's most interesting periods.

But one question hangs over it all: are these games still fun to play?

The collection includes Alien Breed (1991), Alien Breed: Special Edition '92, Alien Breed II: The Horror Continues, Alien Breed: Tower Assault, Alien Breed 3D and Alien Breed 3D II: The Killing Grounds.

In a recent development, the first four are the games most people will remember, and I played more of the classic top-down 2D shooters, with their overhead perspective, maze-like levels, and hordes of aliens waiting around every corner. There's a little Gauntlet in the DNA, a bit of Smash TV, and more than a hint of James Cameron's Aliens. You explore abandoned space stations, collect ammunition, hunt for keys, and try not to get overwhelmed by the growing number of creatures closing in, often because of a brutal respawn system.

According to recent reports, it's a simple formula, but Team17 – now a publisher of some of the best indie games – knew how to make it entertaining. There's a nice rhythm to working through a level, finding supplies and opening up latest areas, although the difficulty can be pretty unforgiving.

According to recent reports, playing those early games now in the 35th Anniversary Collection showcases both the strengths and weaknesses of the series. These games are brutally fun when you take time to learn the maps, play and replay, remember where keys are located, and manage the alien 'breed' and its AI by keeping it locked behind corridor walls.

But it can also become overburdened by the horde; without the right weapons, life is short-lived, and it can be frustrating to waste keys and then not be able to unlock the doors you need, and restart beckons. The original is worse for this; the Special Edition improved, and by Alien Breed II the team had ironed out the kinks, and the game plays with a perfect rhythm. Back in the 90s, we had to play two games and three years to get perfection; on this collection, it's right there.

Some may disagree; I think Alien Breed II, with its visual detail and balanced map design and item placement, is the best of the series, but Tower Assault comes close. The environments offer more variety and a stronger sense of progression, but the second game is the real gem.

Then there's the move into 3D, something I envied back in the day because you needed an Amiga 1200 or Amiga CD32 to run it. Alien Breed 3D arrived in 1995, when everyone wanted to make a Doom-like shooter, and Team17 was keen to prove the Amiga could compete with the growing PC gaming setups and new consoles like PlayStation. It was an ambitious move, especially given the hardware limitations, and the sequel, The Killing Grounds, pushed that idea further but, interestingly, dropped much of the Alien Breed branding and imagery for a more Doom-like aesthetic.

Playing them now is a different experience because a) I can play them and b) they're important games in the story of the Amiga. But being historically interesting and being enjoyable shooters are two very different things.

In a recent development, alien Breed 3D now feels like a tech demo, and it drops much of the series' identity: the 3D experience. I remember the impact this game had back in '95, especially for Amiga owners used to pushing the computer's graphics to the limit. But is it a good game? Not really. It's a decent Doom clone, but even in '95 it couldn't compete with games like Dark Forces.

Alien Breed 3D II is slightly different, though: it plays better today and has a cleaner, more focused Doom-like appeal, but much of Alien Breed's visual hooks and identity have been ironed out in favour of what feels like a solid, standalone Doom clone.

Recent findings suggest that but playing all the games back to back in the 35th Anniversary Collection is more interesting than just replaying games I loved on my Amiga, because it indicates how a series develops, how improvements are inched forward, how trends and pressures pull on a brand and force upcoming directions. This is where the collection excels.

If you're buying this collection purely for the games, you might be missing its biggest selling point.

The Virtual Museum is an interactive archive that lets you explore the history of Alien Breed through original box art, advertising, concept work, soundtracks and interviews with the people who made the games. It also includes a timeline and material from projects that never saw the light of day, which I've spent far more time exploring than I imagined. It includes a cancelled PSP game that looks like it could have struck the right balance between 'modern' 3D and classic Alien Breed corridor shootouts, and an Alien Breed RTS that would have used randomised levels and X-Com-like gameplay.

Industry observers note that I love seeing this sort of material included in retro collections. It's easy to throw a few old games into an emulator and call it a day, but preserving gaming history takes more than making sure an old title still runs on a modern console.

Alien Breed was part of Team17's early identity, and this archive gives you a better idea of how the studio developed the series, what it was trying to achieve and how its ambitions changed as gaming moved from 2D to 3D.

The collection includes interviews with the original artists and developers, plus art, models, design docs, and even videos showing concept art progressing from sketch to final painting. Those cancelled games offer a wealth of content rarely seen in retro game collections, including level maps, concept art, and even gameplay demos.

The original games also get welcome additions that make them more accessible. Twin-stick controls are supported across the 2D and 3D titles; you can choose from display formats, CRT filters, and screen bezels, and save states mean you don't have to commit to a full session every time you sit down.

The collection also includes local co-op in supporting games, online Rush Mode and a new solo Horde Mode. These additions are useful, particularly if you want to play with someone else or fancy a more immediate arcade challenge.

It has been revealed that I've spent time digging into the setup menus and fiddling around; for example, there's a choice of CRT scanlines, but also scanline transparency levels. There's no remake-versus-original graphics mode, because these aren't remakes but excellent emulations. I find the new DualSense control layout feels right; it's modern without ruining the series' distinct feel, and you still get that Alien Breed thing of hugging corridor walls.

It has been revealed that there are some compromises, though. The original games have been preserved in their original formats, and while that's crucial, it also means some of their limitations come along for the ride. The 3D games in particular will test your patience if you're used to modern shooters because you need to play within the game's little 3D window (it's not as modernised as the Star Wars Dark Forces Remake, for example), and the collection could have done more to make those games 'modern'. But then that's the knife's edge a collection like this runs: we want the games we had 35 years ago, but we expect today's features; we can't have it both ways.

Sources indicate that as a fan back in the day, I love having all these games together on a modern console, partly because they're still good, but also because I never got to play the 3D entries. Alien Breed is an key part of Team17's history, and the collection does a good job of showing how the series evolved across six releases.

But I don't think the games themselves have aged equally well. The top-down shooters still have something to offer if you enjoy old-school arcade games, with Alien Breed II being the one I've been returning to more than the others. The 3D games are more difficult to recommend as anything other than historical curiosities.

But it's the archive that makes this collection worthwhile. The artwork, interviews and unreleased projects give Alien Breed a context that simply playing the games can't provide. It's a chance to look at a British studio's creative development over an exciting period for gaming, a time when Team17 could have been swallowed but it thrived, and that's worth celebrating.

If, like me, you grew up with an Amiga, there's plenty here to enjoy. If you've never played Alien Breed before, however, I'd approach it as a piece of gaming history rather than a newly discovered classic because not every game in the collection is a banger.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy Studio Gang.

Architecture practice Studio Gang has completed a women’s conference centre overlooking Geneva Lake in Wisconsin, with three irregularly shaped buildings informed by the site’s oak forest.

Located outside of Chicago on a lakeside hill, the Women’s Leadership Center contains meeting spaces for established and emerging women in leadership roles to gather and “ideate solutions to complex challenges within their industries”.

It has been revealed that “Women leaders spend much of their careers in rooms that weren’t designed with them in mind,” said the center’s founder Ann Drake, former CEO of supply chain provider DSC Logistics. “I wanted to build one that was.”.

Studio Gang noted key elements of the design were sustainability – with strategies such as a mass timber structure – and responding to the ecology of the site through gently curving volumes and wide-open windows.

“We designed the Women’s Leadership Center to respect and learn from its surrounding forest ecology while allowing community, leadership, and collaborative problem-solving to thrive,” mentioned Studio Gang founding partner Jeanne Gang.

“Locally sourced materials, mass timber, and low-carbon concrete minimise the buildings’ carbon footprint, while the landscape helps to repair the site’s ecology and enhance its biodiversity.”.

The campus contains three main buildings — the circular Council building that functions as the main meeting space, the Lodge, which is made of three interconnected volumes, and the Cabin, a smaller building that contains accommodations.

White oak wood harvested on-site, a dark wood cladding and natural Wisconsin stone were used throughout all three buildings to “reflect the tones and textures of the forest”, according to the studio.

The Council building is arranged around a central courtyard and garden that doubles as a rainwater-collection site.

Its rooms, including a larger lecture hall and meeting room, fan outwards around the courtyard and are lined with floor-to-ceiling windows, while a heavy timber structure creates a series of skylights at the entrance.

According to recent reports, A walkway leads out the back of the Council building towards the Lodge. The building contains more casual meeting and socialising spaces, such as a Great Room arranged around a fireplace.

It also contains a mass-timber structure above this space, which is lined with skylights. Outdoor terraces overlook Geneva Lake, while the building’s green roof contains a “coffee nook” and patios for seating.

Tucked off into a corner of the site, the Cabin building contains several bedrooms across two levels, as well as utility spaces such as a laundry room.

Its lower level contains a dining area and living area, which double as additional, more intimate gathering spaces.

Fully accessible ramps interconnect all three structures and lead down to the water bank, where they end in a pier.

Elsewhere, Studio Gang recently completed an open-air theatre in upstate Fresh York and a Denver hotel.

Photography courtesy Studio Gang.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Both Rubens and his erstwhile assistant Van Dyck venerated Titian as the very prince of painters.” So writes the Titian expert Peter Humfrey in the catalogue for Dickinson’s impressive newly introduced exhibition, Titian, Rubens, Van Dyck, which opened last night and runs until 18th December at 58 Jermyn Street, London.

Recent findings suggest that simon Dickinson and his son Milo have brought together two paintings by Titian, two by Rubens and nine by Van Dyck for the show, all from private collections and most for sale, priced between around £400,000 and over £3m. At the heart of the show is the relationship between the three painters, principally the influence of Titian on the two younger, Flemish painters.

The exhibition, one of the most ambitious staged by the gallery in its 33-year history, is accompanied by an extensive catalogue including essays from Humfrey alongside the Belgian art historians Koenraad Jonckheere, a professor in Northern Renaissance and Baroque art at Ghent University, and Katlijne Van der Stighelen, a Rubens expert.

While works by Titian, Rubens and Van Dyck are “very, very difficult to find”, Milo Dickinson notes, there are still some at large thanks to all three being extremely prolific. “Titian was this great role model to Rubens and then Van Dyck, both as a man who was a successful artist throughout his life, courted by major patrons, but also as a painter: the colours he used, the compositions he devised,” Dickinson says. Rubens, for instance, “spent several months just copying paintings by Titian in Madrid, which had been bought by Phillip II of Spain.” As for Van Dyck, the sketchbook he took around Italy when he was a young man is full of annotated studies of Titians.

The exhibition includes several recent rediscoveries, most made after cleaning, with the catalogue outlining the arguments in favour of the attributions made by various experts.

Peter Paul Rubens, Study of the young Anthony van Dyck (around 1616-7).

According to recent reports, courtesy: Simon C. Dickinson Ltd.

Among them is what is thought to be a late self-portrait by Titian, variously dated by scholars to between 1546-47 to 1560. The attribution has been long debated by scholars, Milo Dickinson states. Everett Fahy, the American art historian and former director of the Frick who died in 2018, first proposed the attribution to Titian in 2009 when the painting emerged—filthy—from a French private collection. The oil on canvas, small at 44cm by 33cm, was sold for $69,850 at Sotheby's New York in 2024, catalogued as “attributed to Titian”. It has subsequently been cleaned, X-rayed and further studied. Now, Dickinson says, “various scholars—Peter Humfrey, Nicholas Penny and Ian Kennedy—have written on it and debated the dating of it because [if the attribution is correct] it would make it one of only three accepted self-portraits by Titian”, alongside those in the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin and that in the Prado, Madrid. The painting, which has been in a UK private collection since 2024, is now priced at £1.5m.

Another find is a Rubens head study which is now thought to depict a young Anthony van Dyck, based on dating, the sitter’s distinctive features and comparison with van Dyck’s self-portraits. The oil on panel, which measures 43cm by 35cm, was bought by the current owner at Sotheby’s Paris last November as part of the sale of the collection of the British property billionaire Manny Davidson. Catalogued as a Head Study of a Boy by Rubens, it sold for €744,000. With fitting circularity, Davidson had bought the painting as “attributed to Rubens” in 2007 from Simon Dickinson in 2007, who had spent several years trying to prove it was by Rubens.

The study had been thought to date to around 1614, when Van Dyck would have been only 14 or 15 years old, younger than the boy depicted here with his wispy stubble. But the Louvre, which holds the other half of this double head study, has recently argued that its sketch probably dates to 1616-17. “That got us thinking,” Dickinson notes. “Once you've seen it cleaned, you realise the hair colour, the distinct shape of the face, the lips, the shape of the nose, they're totally concurrent with what Van Dyck looked like in his self-portraits.” He adds that Jonckheere and Van der Stighelen support the identity of the sitter as being van Dyck, alongside other scholars. The head study is for sale, price undisclosed.

Brunaille equestrian study by van Dyck (around 1629-32).

Courtesy Simon C. Dickinson Ltd.

Yet another post-clean rediscovery is a study by van Dyck for the equestrian portrait of Albert de Ligne, Prince of Arenberg and Barbançon (around 1629-32) which hangs in Holkham Hall, Norfolk. It is one of several similar brunaille studies, one of which is the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. Another of these sketches, presumed to be the original, had been in the De Craecker collection in the 19th century but had since gone missing. “Then this one appeared in an American private collection and it was pretty clear, upon seeing it cleaned, that this was the original and the other versions were copies done in Van Dyck's studio by assistants.” Dickinson says.

It has been revealed that he adds that “the sheer quality, the way that he uses highlights, the abbreviated forms” in this version are superior when compared to the others. The pentimenti (revisions) in this, typical of Van Dyck, have also become clearly visible over time, Dickinson says, particularly the adjusted position of the horses head and front legs. The American collector, who bought it in 2014, is now selling the sketch through Dickinson, with an asking price in the region of £500,000.

Industry observers note that at the top end of the price range is a friendship portrait by Titian, offered at £3m. Portrait of a young man with a gloved hand (around 1550) is thought to have been the portrait by Titian that is mentioned in van Dyck’s posthumous inventory. It was last publicly exhibited in 1939-40.

The exhibition will travel to New York for the Master Drawings New York art fair in (29 January–6 February 2027).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The New York Times has banned freelance photographers from using the app because of a difficulty in knowing when it uses generative AI.
  • There's an easy solution, but will Adobe want to introduce it?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we were genuinely impressed with some of the new AI features in Photoshop 2027, from Generative Restyle to Relight. But just a couple of weeks after its release, the latest version of the industry-standard image editing software is facing a reputational crisis.

The New York Times has banned freelance photographers from using the app because of a difficulty in knowing when it uses generative AI. That's just one publication, but the news has made a major impact, and the significance is clear: owners may not be 100% sure when they are or aren't using generative AI to edit an image.

There's an easy solution, but will Adobe want to introduce it?

Industry observers note that the New York Times wrote in an email to freelance photographers that the newest version of Photoshop “utilizes generative AI in ways that may not be apparent to users. Their use can result in metadata misidentifying photos as AI-generated.” As a result photographers have been told not to use the latest version of the software.

In photojournalism, it's an ethical issue. Images need to reflect reality, so editing is usually relatively limited. The inadvertent use of generative AI also brings with it the risk of an "AI content" tag on social media, which could lead people to question a report, and could severely damage to the reputation of both the photographer and any media outlet reporting news with an image flagged as AI.

Sources indicate that the most obvious solution would be an AI-off switch. Digital artists, designers and those photographers who want to use generative AI tools in Photoshop could turn it on. Photojournalists, documentary photographers, and anyone who simply doesn't want to use generative AI or risk being shamed with an AI content tag, can turn it off.

It has been revealed that other software developers have done just that. Canva added an AI off Switch last week, and Maxon has included the ability to turn off its new generative AI features in Cinema 4D and ZBrush. It's a simple mechanism that can be flicked on or off at any time, and the gesture helps offer reassurance to those consumers who oppose AI.

The question is whether Adobe will be willing to follow this lead, or if it will fear that a switch would call its direction into question or discourage people from using the AI tools it wants to promote.

Adobe didn't immediately respond to an invitation to comment.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A contemporary take on Ukrainian vernacular buildings and a preschool in Estonia are among the winners of the Thermory Design Awards 2026, which celebrate the versatility of thermally modified wood.
  • Of 78 submissions from 23 countries, four winning projects have been selected in the competition’s fifth annual edition, covering the categories of interior, tiny and private house, residential, commercial and public building, and wellness and spa.
  • Thermory thermowood is wood that has been modified using heat and steam with no added chemicals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A contemporary take on Ukrainian vernacular buildings and a preschool in Estonia are among the winners of the Thermory Design Awards 2026, which celebrate the versatility of thermally modified wood.

Of 78 submissions from 23 countries, four winning projects have been selected in the competition’s fifth annual edition, covering the categories of interior, tiny and private house, residential, commercial and public building, and wellness and spa.

Thermory thermowood is wood that has been modified using heat and steam with no added chemicals.

The treatment enhances the material’s dimensional stability and reduces moisture uptake compared with untreated wood, according to Thermory.

The winner of the interior category is a trio of Ukrainian guesthouses collectively named Under the Reed Roof, designed by Kyiv-based studio YOD Group.

Each guesthouse comprises a glass-walled volume at the base, topped by a tapered thatched roof with exaggerated proportions.

While the exterior of these roofs is made with traditional reeds, the interiors are lined with thermo-ash shingles, arranged to create a tactile effect that is repeated on the front doors.

These highlight the interplay between the interior’s traditional and contemporary design elements, contrasting materials, and the balance between the structure’s openness and enclosure.

“The project stood out to the jury for its exceptionally coherent concept, in which architecture and interior elements come together to form a harmonious whole,” mentioned Thermory.

Winning in the tiny and private house category was Marker Architecture‘s Flooded Gums project, a flood-resilient dwelling built on working farmland.

The building features thermo-ash cladding and thermo-spruce decking, owing to the materials’ robustness and aesthetic merits.

“What particularly impressed the jury was the honesty and clarity of the architecture,” said Thermory of the project.

“Rather than concealing its construction, the project makes its structural logic visible, with every element serving a purpose: the result is a modest yet highly refined building that strikes a compelling balance between aesthetics, functionality and its natural setting,” it added.

Estonia’s Rakke Kindergarten secured the win in the residential, commercial and public building category, thanks to what Thermory describes as local studio Arhitekt Must‘s “cohesive and imaginative design”.

Thermo-spruce cladding, thermo-pine posts and thermo-pine decking all feature in the design, enhancing both its functionality and visual appeal.

The building’s function as an educational environment is made distinctive by the space’s inventive ceiling, which is composed of the short thermo-pine posts, arranged in a way that creates an engaging optical illusion.

“This unexpected architectural gesture elevates a functional space into something distinctive, demonstrating how thoughtful detailing can shape the character and experience of an entire building,” said Thermory.

Finally, the winner of the wellness and spa category is a sauna within the Estonian Embassy in Berlin, designed by interior studio AERIS.

The interiors feature statement walls covered in custom-made oak shingles, which, being circular and slightly overlapping, resemble fish scales.

These are joined by thermo-alder benches and walls, creating a cohesive scheme of timber details that integrate neatly with the lighting design.

“The harmonious interplay of materials, surfaces and light imbues the space with a contemporary edge while retaining the intimacy and warmth of a traditional sauna,” remarked Thermory.

“Although vastly different in character and purpose, the winning projects share a creative and unconventional approach to design,” it added.

“Each places wood at the heart of its architectural expression, combining imaginative thinking with meticulous attention to detail.”.

The 2026 instalment of the competition was judged by a diverse international jury of architects and Thermory representatives, including Kärt Kanarbik, Thermory’s architectural project manager; Lars Skjølstrup Østergaard, lead design architect at Henning Larsen; Sami Rintala, professor and architect at Rintala Eggertsson Architects; Jaan Port, architect and partner at PIN Arhitektid; and Tõnis Kalve, architect at ByKalve and Thermory project sales architect.

To learn more about Thermory, visit its website.

#148890. Wait, the Grand Theft Auto logo is based on a free font inspired by a game show?

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (829 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Creativebloq ↗ Open Full Page

Wait, the Grand Theft Auto logo is based on a free font inspired by a game show?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (829 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that even if you haven't spent every waking hour of the past seven days immersed in the world of Leonida, you've sure seen a lot of the GTA logo lately.
  • For long-time fans of series, the GTA VI logo is a familiar design with the same core wordmark that's been in use since Grand Theft Auto III.
  • In a recent development, the original Grand Theft Auto logo created by The Designers Republic for the first game's marketing featured cartoonish stars and flames for a '70s vibe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that even if you haven't spent every waking hour of the past seven days immersed in the world of Leonida, you've sure seen a lot of the GTA logo lately. Along with the Vice City palette of pastel pinks, blues and sunset oranges, the logo has been everywhere, from developer Rockstar Games' billboards and murals to those GTA VI brand reactions.

For long-time fans of series, the GTA VI logo is a familiar design with the same core wordmark that's been in use since Grand Theft Auto III. But older readers who have never played GTA might also find it strangely familiar. That could be because it's based on a free typeface that was inspired by a very different kind of game.

In a recent development, the original Grand Theft Auto logo created by The Designers Republic for the first game's marketing featured cartoonish stars and flames for a '70s vibe. It was replaced by a simpler three-letter GTA logo for the second game, in the franchise. It was Grand Theft Auto III in 2001 that introduced the design we know today.

In a recent development, the logo is largely based on Pricedown, a free typeface developed by the Canadian designer Raymond Larabie and published by Typodermic. In his post about the history of the font on the foundry's website, Raymond says his intention was to closely reinterpret Pinto Flare, a display face made for Franklin Photolettering in the late 1960s and best known for its use in The Price Is Right logo.

"I kept the boxy structure and the odd unicase letterforms with swash descenders, but I drew my version harder and more angular compared to Pinto Flare’s softer feel," he writes.

Industry observers note that raymond states he released Pricedown on 30 November 1997. That was just two days after the first GTA came out for windows. And the coincidences don't end there. He says that when the font was later chosen by Rockstar's office in Latest York, he happened to be working as an art director at Rockstar Toronto. His colleagues weren't aware that someone working at the company had designed the font.

In a recent development, so the world's most expensive video game has a logo based on a free font? And it works: the chunky letterforms with their rounded corners work perfectly achieving easy readability while fitting into the rest of the game's branding.

But it would be a simplification to say that Pricedown is all there is to the GTA logo. Ultimately, Rockstar modified the letterforms and arranged them to make them work as a logo design. The three words of the franchise's name are clustered tightly in an almost square block, the 'r' and 'h' conjoin, and a black stroke provides separation against coloured backgrounds.

Recent findings suggest that ink traps replaced overlapping curves, and the bowls seem to have been made more open to improve readability. This all helps the wordmark to function as a single cohesive unit.

An additional touch has been added for each game in the form of the numbering: a pink neon sign-like script for Vice City, tattoo-like blackletter type for San Andreas, the V that recalls US currency design for GTA V.

Considering Grand Theft Auto's satire of US culture and society, it seems fitting for it to have a logo inspired by the identity of one of the country's longest-running TV series (see our pick of the best GTA VI Easter eggs for examples of how the game references pop culture and its own legacy).

According to recent reports, looking for the font? The original Pricedown, now called Pricedown Black is available free for desktop use, and you can download it directly from Typodermic. Raymond later expanded the font into a complete typeface family with other weights. To use those, you'll need to buy a licence. You can find them at MyFonts.

For more on the game of the biggest video game in history, check out our interviews with Rockstar Games' art team on GTA VI's environmental storytelling and the building design in GTA VI.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hoor Al Qasimi, one of the preeminent figures of contemporary art in the Middle East, has been named curator of the Venice Biennale's next art exhibition, the Biennale has announced.

Following this year's edition, which was curated by the late Cameroon-born curator Koyo Kouoh, the appointment of Al Qasimi, from the United Arab Emirates (UAE), marks the second consecutive edition in which a woman from outside the Western art world has been chosen for the role.

Al Qasimi was born into the royal family of the port city of Sharjah and is the daughter of Sultan bin Muhammad Al Qasimi, the current leader of the emirate of Sharjah.

Sources indicate that she has been involved in the Sharjah Biennial since 2003, when she curated the exhibition's sixth edition after completing her undergraduate studies at the Slade School of Fine Art in London. In 2009, she founded the Sharjah Art Foundation, a public art organisation that promotes and funds contemporary art collaborations in the emirate and internationally, including organising the Sharjah Biennial.

In a recent development, she holds board positions for numerous other arts organisations, including the International Biennial Association, Sharjah Museums Authority, Sharjah Architecture Triennial and University of the Arts Sharjah. She has also curated major exhibitions including the Lahore Biennale in 2020, the Aichi Triennale in Japan in 2025, and this year's edition of the Biennale of Sydney.

Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, president of the Venice Biennale, indicates in a statement that Al Qasimi's work gives “voice to stories and sensibilities shaped by research and the unexpected”.

He adds: “Her work brings together a profound attentiveness to deep-rooted memory and its legacies, an open perspective on the intricate complexities of the present, and a rare ability to listen to places and their people...These are qualities that we feel are particularly close to La Biennale’s vision”.

Buttafuoco, a right-leaning journalist and intellectual who was born and raised in Catania in Sicily, reportedly converted to Islam in 2015, adopting the name Giafar al-Siqilli (“Jafar the Sicilian”) in a reference to the Arab-Sicilian general associated with the Fatimid conquest of North Africa.

In a recent development, since becoming president of the Biennale in 2024, he has sometimes championed art from the Middle East. In 2025, under his watch, Qatar declared it would launch a national pavilion at the Biennale. A temporary structure was used for the most recent architecture and art biennales; the completed pavilion building will be the first permanent addition to the Giardini, one of the Biennale’s two main venues, in 30 years.

In a statement, Al Qasimi says that the Biennale “continues to be a critical space to engage with the work of influential artists and curators”, adding that she was “honoured” to be appointed as curator.

Al Qasimi could not immediately be reached for comment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the FBI is seeking a warrant to search electronic devices belonging to a Grand Rapids man accused of stealing art from two Michigan art museums. The news was reported by multiple outlets, including MLive.

Sources indicate that according to a federal affidavit, Mikolai Augustine Stasiulewicz, 27, allegedly stole a color lithograph by artist Ellsworth Kelly, from Western Michigan University’s (WMU) Richmond Center for the Visual Arts on June 23. A worker notified WMU police that the work was missing, and Stasiulewicz, who was caught on surveillance video carrying the framed print, was identified through facial-recognition analysis by Michigan State Police. Related Articles 13th-Century Carving Stolen by Art Thief 'Eric the Belgian' Recovered in the UK Stolen Picasso Prints Found Under Pile of Clothes in French Riviera Apartment.

Sources indicate that stasiulewicz is also alleged to have stolen a 16th-century Albrecht Dürer print from the Grand Rapids Art Museum (GRAM) on July 2. According to the FBI, he had been seen at the museum on June 17, “in what appeared to be a pre-theft surveillance visit.” Between the two thefts, he is accused of entering nonpublic areas at the Muskegon Museum of Art on June 25; however, Muskegon police said he didn’t take anything.

Recent findings suggest that the FBI, which eventually took over the case, learned during its investigations that Stasiulewicz had met with a man on July 8 at the Gun Lake Casino Resort in Wayland, Michigan. Surveillance video demonstrates him leaving with an unknown amount of cash.

Stasiulewicz was found dead in his home on July 30. According to the Kent County Medical Examiner’s Office, he died of a morphine overdose on July 26. Although the office’s autopsy report rules the death an accident, it also notes that “the decedent is currently under investigation by the FBI for involvement in an art gallery theft,” and that a brother had told police that may have played a part in his death.

Four artworks, including the Kelly, valued at $10,000 and the Dürer, valued at $10,000–$20,000, were found at the home the next day.

In a recent development, on Monday, November 23, the FBI sought a warrant to search Stasiulewicz’s cellphone and laptop computer to determine if any others were involved in the thefts. “In my training and experience, and that of the Art Crime Team, phones and computers like the devices will often be used to communicate with co-conspirators,” FBI Special Agent Evan Alkema wrote in the federal affidavit. “They may contain evidence of communications about what art pieces to steal, negotiations for sale prices, and arrangements to transfer and ‘fence’ the stolen works.”.

Since its inception in 2004, the FBI’s Art Crime Team, which handles cases involving the theft, forgery, and trafficking of art and cultural artifacts, has recovered more than 20,000 objects valued at $1 billion.

Stasiulewicz was an amateur artist who studied at the Interlochen Center of the Arts, the FBI said.

Assemble covers miniature agricultural buildings in intense blue pigment for Building Blue exhibition in Tokyo

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architecture collective Assemble has created small, climbable cedar buildings that “play with scale” to showcase a new pigment, made from industrial waste by design studio Matter at hand, at Tokyo‘s SKAC gallery.
  • With the exhibition, the UK-based collective said it aimed to “explore the transformation of landscape through colour and into colour”.
  • The exhibition was jointly created by the two studios to showcase the upcoming pigment, developed by Matter at hand from local waste material, on the miniature buildings made by Assemble.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Daisuke Shima.

Architecture collective Assemble has created small, climbable cedar buildings that “play with scale” to showcase a new pigment, made from industrial waste by design studio Matter at hand, at Tokyo‘s SKAC gallery.

With the exhibition, the UK-based collective said it aimed to “explore the transformation of landscape through colour and into colour”.

The exhibition was jointly created by the two studios to showcase the upcoming pigment, developed by Matter at hand from local waste material, on the miniature buildings made by Assemble.

The blue hue was manufactured by Japanese firm Nikken to be used in the Play Earth Park – a campsite designed by Assemble that is presently under development in rural Japan.

“The pigment was essentially created by analysing local material waste streams in Toyama and exploring what kind of different colours could be produced from them,” Matter at hand founder Lewis Jones told Dezeen.

“In the end, the blue uses a combination of rice husk ash, limestone filter dust, recycled glass and copper, which are mixed together with water to form a thick clay-like paste and then heated in an electric kiln to around 950ºC,” he continued.

“The materials react to form a new crystal phase – known as cuprorivaite, which is bright blue.”.

To show it off, Assemble constructed three miniature houses from Japanese cedar that draw on the agricultural buildings found close to where the pigment material was sourced. The houses were named The Hut, The Tower and The Bird.

“The form of the structures plays with the agricultural buildings within the dispersed settlement of rural Toyama; these buildings evolve over time, adapting to what’s needed, often evolving interesting geometries,” Assemble co-founder Maria Lisogorskaya told Dezeen.

“We tried to play with scale and make the buildings surreal, creating miniature versions of them for play.”.

It has been revealed that the buildings have deliberately simple yet evocative geometries that nod to the structures that inspired them. Among them is a barn-like building surrounded by hay bales.

Assemble’s aim was for visitors to be able to climb and explore the structures.

“We hope that the buildings are climbed on and inhabited; and this exhibition is the beginning of the structures’ life as a play space outside SKWAT,” Lisogorskaya stated.

“The spirit of resourcefulness, fun, and reimagining of our environments is at the core of the project and we look forward to seeing how the structures are used in ways we didn’t expect.”.

The exhibition, which also showcases raw materials used to create the blue colour and products covered in it, is on show in Skwat Kameari Art Centre (SKAC’s) Park gallery in Kameari, Tokyo.

Assemble said it chose to showcase it here as it feels the gallery has a similar spirit to its own UK bases.

“We think SKAC is an amazing interdisciplinary space, and its spirit resonates with how we have set up our studios and labs in London and Liverpool,” Lisogorskaya stated.

“Bringing together design, material experimentation with other arts practices as a more satisfying and richer way of being in the city,” she continued.

SKAC recently opened two new gallery spaces, Material Matters (MM) and Space III, as part of a major extension.

The east Tokyo gallery has previously shown exhibitions including anime-informed chairs by Kwangho Lee and reading spaces by Herzog & de Meuron.

Building Blue is at SKAC, 3-26-4 Kameari, Katsushika-ku, Tokyo 125-0002, from 7 November 2026 to 28 February 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Photography by Daisuke Shima.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Activists against women’s right to choose in relation to their reproductive rights protested a sculpture by Shahzia Sikander in St. Louis this week, calling for the removal of the 18-foot-tall work titled Witness (2023).

According to recent reports, as reported by St. Louis’s First Alert 4, protesters associating the sculpture with pro-choice abortion rights gathered outside the home base of Rung for Women, a nonprofit devoted to women’s career development that hosts it. As the organization describes itself on its website, “Too many women are unfulfilled, unhappy, and underpaid in their jobs, but afraid to take the leap into the unknown. We designed a program to guide motivated women through a process to start working in exciting careers and get paid what they’re worth.” Related Articles Shahzia Sikander's Animated Film Selected for M+ Facade Commission in Hong Kong Shahzia Sikander Indicates She Won't Repair Beheaded Sculpture in Texas: 'A Testament to Hatred'.

First Alert 4 quoted an activist with a group called Students for Life America associating Sikander’s sculpture with the overturning of Roe v. Wade in 2022. “Her skirt spells Hava, which is Eve, the first female rebel, to breathe life,” remarked Reagan Barklage, who related the work to the late US Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg. “It’s just, you do not need to kill your children in order to breathe life. That’s actually the exact opposite of what that means.”.

It has been revealed that she continued: “We’re alarmed that this is what they’re choosing to use to represent our city. We do not stand for these pro-abortion rights. And we’re trying to stand for women and true empowerment.”.

A counterprotester thought otherwise. “We’re here because this organization that’s located on this block has every right to display whatever artwork they want on their own property,” said Leslie Zacks, who spoke of the protest in the context of a recently failed amendment that would have reinstated a near-total abortion ban. “The reality of the situation is that the people in Missouri have twice had the opportunity to voice their preferences with regards to the abortion issue and have made it very, very clear with increasing majority where their preferences are.”.

In a recent development, rung for Women issued a statement saying the organization “respects the right of individuals to express their views about art, including those that differ from our own. We recognize that Witness has prompted strong reactions and respect the sincerely held beliefs of those who have expressed concern. We remain proud to host this work by Shahzia Sikander at Rung for Women.”.

Sources indicate that the same sculpture by Sikander was the subject of heated protest in Texas in 2024, when it was decried by a group that called it “satanic” before it was to go on view at the University of Houston. After an opening and artist talk related to the work were subsequently canceled, Sikander stated, “Art should be about discourse and not censorship. Shame on those that silence artists.”.

An attempt by ARTnews to reach the artist was not immediately successful.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The phrase "finding your tribe" was thrown around profusely during the conference, and while I find the term mildly ickworthy, it bears truth.
